Laboratory respirometry trials conducted on adult Smith (Pseudoeurycea smithi) at a stable temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C] revealed a maximal resting metabolic rate of 0.0018 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 0.0018 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This exceptionally low oxygen consumption is among the lowest recorded for any plethodontid salamander of comparable size and reflects the pronounced metabolic suppression typical of neotropical bolitoglossines inhabiting cool, high-elevation cloud forests. These measurements were taken from post-absorptive individuals during their inactive diurnal period to ensure standard conditions. The rate of 0.0018 milliliters of oxygen per hour aligns closely with predictions based on the species' modest adult body mass and its sedentary, fossorial lifestyle. Such a reduced metabolic demand is likely an adaptation to the consistently low environmental temperatures and unpredictable prey availability characteristic of its montane habitat, allowing the species to thrive on a limited energy budget.

Embryological studies of Pseudoeurycea smithi have clarified the early life history of this secretive salamander. Field-collected egg masses, maintained at a constant temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], required approximately 110 days [ab = approximately 110 days] to complete development and hatch. This protracted incubation period is typical for direct-developing plethodontids from high-elevation environments, where low temperatures substantially slow embryonic metabolism. Neonates emerge as fully formed, terrestrial miniatures, having bypassed the free-living larval stage entirely. The wet weight at birth was determined to be 0.0141 grams [Wwb = 0.0141 grams], a value that was mathematically derived from the original egg diameter measurement of approximately 3 millimeters by calculating the volume of a sphere. This exceedingly small birth size represents the lowest extreme of neonatal mass among terrestrial plethodontids and imposes significant constraints on early juvenile survival.

Adults of Pseudoeurycea smithi attain a remarkably uniform ultimate wet weight of 8.49 grams [Wwi = 8.49 grams], a value consistent across both sexes in museum specimen series. This relatively modest adult size places Smith among the smaller members of the genus Pseudoeurycea, a group that spans a considerable range of body masses. The longevity record for this species, under simulated natural thermal conditions maintained at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], extends to approximately 18.5 years [am = approximately 18.5 years]. Such an extended lifespan is exceptional for a terrestrial salamander of this body size and is characteristic of organisms adhering to a slow life-history strategy, where delayed reproduction and low annual metabolic expenditures are coupled with extended somatic maintenance. The maximum recorded lifespan of approximately 18.5 years underscores the profound influence of cool, stable environments on the actuarial aging schedules of these animals.

For female Pseudoeurycea smithi, detailed captive observations conducted at 15 °C [T = 15 °C] have quantified the time required to attain reproductive competence. The interval from the completion of metamorphosis to the onset of puberty was recorded as approximately 1460 days [tp = approximately 1460 days]. at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]This lengthy period of almost exactly four years reflects a remarkably slow pace of sexual maturation, even by plethodontid standards. During this extended juvenile phase, individuals allocate nearly all available resources to somatic growth and the accumulation of energy reserves necessary to support future reproductive events. The substantial duration of 1460 days after metamorphosis until the achievement of puberty likely represents an adaptive response to the unpredictable resource environment of the cloud forest, ensuring that females begin breeding only when they have attained a sufficient body condition.

Reproductive output in Pseudoeurycea smithi is constrained by both its small body size and the energetics of direct development. Under the same thermal regime of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], field records indicate that sexually mature females produce a single clutch of eggs each year [F_R_i = single clutch of eggs each year], with each clutch containing approximately 100 offspring [N_R_i = each clutch containing approximately 100 offspring], yielding a maximum reproductive rate of 100 offspring per year [Ri = 100 offspring per year]. The energetic burden of producing large, yolky, terrestrial eggs is substantial for a salamander weighing only 8.49 grams [Wwi = 8.49 grams], and the low fecundity documented here aligns with the species' overall strategy of investing heavily in the survival of each individual offspring through an extended incubation period.
